article_title: The moderating role of SES on genetic differences in educational achievement in the Netherlands
citation: Eveline L. de Zeeuw, Kees-Jan Kan, Catharina E. M. van Beijsterveldt, Hamdi Mbarek, Jouke-Jan Hottenga, Gareth E. Davies, Michael C. Neale, Conor V. Dolan and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2019). The moderating role of SES on genetic differences in educational achievement in the Netherlands. npj Science of Learning 4:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0052-2
title: Use polygenic scores alongside parental SES to identify children at elevated risk of low educational achievement
description: The article proposes that because a child's PGS is measured at the individual level rather than the family level, it "has added value to SES in predicting which children are at risk for lower EA". Children at double risk, through family background and genetic predisposition, could be targeted by policies such as extra educational programs to reduce inequality in educational outcomes.
requirements: Genetic data of the quality used in the study (genome-wide SNP data with quality control) and parental SES information
constraints: The PGS explains only part of the genetic variance because it is limited by the GWAS on which it is based
The sample over-represented children from high SES backgrounds relative to the Dutch population
target_learning_goals: Educational achievement (scholastic knowledge including language and mathematical skills)
examples: The study used PGSs constructed from a GWAS meta-analysis of educational attainment, corrected for population stratification, in 2335 Dutch children with parental SES data
key_sources: Eveline L. de Zeeuw, Kees-Jan Kan, Catharina E. M. van Beijsterveldt, Hamdi Mbarek, Jouke-Jan Hottenga, Gareth E. Davies, Michael C. Neale, Conor V. Dolan and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2019). The moderating role of SES on genetic differences in educational achievement in the Netherlands. npj Science of Learning 4:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0052-2

article_title: Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy?
citation: Peter M. Visscher. (2022). Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00124-z
title: Use polygenic scores in education policy with caution: the author argues they could allow fairer comparisons across individuals than existing performance-based tracking, but such personalised education is not widely endorsed
description: The article's forward-looking policy discussion argues that because existing tracking methods are highly selective on cognitive performance and therefore indirectly already selective on genetic factors, "Measuring these factors directly through a PGS would allow a fairer comparison across individuals that is not influenced by their socio-economic background". At the same time, the author acknowledges that tracking individuals using their genetic predictor for cognitive ability — a "personalised education" approach — is clearly not endorsed widely. The principle therefore records both the proposed use and its stated social constraint.
requirements: Reliable and sufficiently powerful polygenic scores for cognitive ability and educational attainment
constraints: The article states such a personalised-education approach is clearly not endorsed widely
target_learners: primary and secondary school students facing tracking or streaming decisions
target_learning_goals: fairer educational placement and reduced inequality of opportunity
examples: The author cites the Dutch national exam used for tracking since his own schooling, employed in the Knigge et al. study and in many countries, as indirectly already selective on genetic factors
key_sources: Peter M. Visscher. (2022). Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00124-z

article_title: The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings
citation: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y
title: Use PGS alongside progress monitoring as a strategic learning-disability screener, choosing either- or both-cutoff rules according to the school's priority
description: The article recommends polygenic scores be considered not for individualized instruction but as an inexpensive, time-efficient additional screening tool within universal screening systems. Schools "could be strategically used to increase either positive or NPV": allowing identification by either measure reduces false negatives, while requiring both measures reduces false positives. The choice depends on the values of the school or locality, and the authors stress results must be communicated as probabilistic risk, not diagnosis.
requirements: Combination with existing progress monitoring tools; accurate communication to teachers and parents that results are not diagnostic; the article also recommends comprehensive cost-benefit analyses before implementation and genetic-counseling-like educational outreach.
constraints: Current PGS effectiveness (~2% for specific measures) limits value; reference samples are predominantly European ancestry, so results apply mainly to students of European ancestry and would likely be greatly decreased for other ancestries; ethical concerns including genetic essentialism and potential misuse against marginalized groups must be addressed first.
target_learners: K-12 students being universally screened for academic risk, especially in early grades
target_learning_goals: Early, accurate identification of students at risk of learning disabilities to guide supplemental intervention
examples: The simulations quantified NPV gains of 0.3–3.4% under the either-cutoff rule and PPV gains of 3.9–13.4% under the both-cutoffs rule, and the authors suggest the either-cutoff approach may be especially beneficial in earlier grades.
key_sources: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y

article_title: Effects on postgraduate-year-I residents of simulation-based learning compared to traditional lecture-style education led by postgraduate-year-II residents: a pilot study.
citation: Yamamoto Akira, Obika Mikako, Mandai Yasuhiro, Murakami Taku, Miyoshi Tomoko, Ino Hideo, Kataoka Hitomi, Otsuka Fumio. (2019). Effects on postgraduate-year-I residents of simulation-based learning compared to traditional lecture-style education led by postgraduate-year-II residents: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1509-y
title: Peer-led simulation program with three calibrated clinical scenarios and debriefing-weighted session structure
description: A one-hour-per-case simulation program for PGY-I residents, taught by volunteer PGY-II residents, built around three scenarios (acute myocardial infarction, multiple injuries, aspiration pneumonia) developed through alpha and beta testing with prior PGY-I input and expert review. Each scenario repeated "case presentation, team discussion, simulation training, and debriefing" (1, 3, 5, and 8 minutes) three times with role rotation, using tools such as SimMan 3G, a monitor, an emergency cart, and a cardiac defibrillator.
requirements: Volunteer PGY-II residents as teaching staff, who received debriefing education before participating
Scenarios calibrated for difficulty, validity, accuracy, and effectiveness through alpha and beta testing
Simulation equipment including high-fidelity patient simulators and real equipment
constraints: Evaluated in a single facility over three one-week orientation periods before clinical practice
target_learners: Postgraduate-year-I medical residents entering clinical practice
target_learning_goals: Initial evaluation and management of the three scenario conditions
examples: Teaching staff presented blood, X-ray, CT, electro-cardiogram, and ultrasound results when requested by trainees; the lecture group received a one-hour one-way lecture on the same cases and goals
key_sources: Yamamoto Akira, Obika Mikako, Mandai Yasuhiro, Murakami Taku, Miyoshi Tomoko, Ino Hideo, Kataoka Hitomi, Otsuka Fumio. (2019). Effects on postgraduate-year-I residents of simulation-based learning compared to traditional lecture-style education led by postgraduate-year-II residents: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1509-y
